scenario_stem:
Marlbrook Outfitters is a private limited company operating 3 clothing stores in Country X, run by managing director Naomi Hargrave for 8 years. In the year to 30 June, revenue was $840,000, cost of sales $462,000, gross profit $378,000, operating expenses $252,000 and profit $126,000; last year revenue was $780,000, gross profit $304,200 and profit $97,500 on a smaller range of premium lines.

Naomi is considering launching a cheaper own-brand clothing range to lift sales and compete with value retailers, or keeping the premium lines her loyal customers prefer. She has asked her accountant to prepare ratio analysis comparing both years for the board, which meets in 6 weeks to approve the own-brand range and decide its pricing and promotion.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross profit margin'.
questions.model_answer: Gross profit margin is the percentage of revenue remaining as gross profit after deducting the cost of sales, calculated as gross profit divided by revenue multiplied by 100; for Marlbrook Outfitters this year, $378,000 divided by $840,000 multiplied by 100 gives 45.0%, up from 39.0% last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin = gross profit / revenue x 100
It shows the percentage of each dollar of revenue kept after cost of sales

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Naomi should use gross profit margin when judging the own-brand proposal.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: gross profit margin shows the percentage of revenue left after the cost of sales, so it reveals how efficiently Marlbrook buys or makes its goods [k]; the margin improved from 39% ($304,200 divided by $780,000) last year to 45% ($378,000 divided by $840,000) this year, evidence that cost control on premium lines is strong [app]. Reason 2: gross profit margin lets Naomi compare lines and judge whether a cheaper own-brand range would still cover the cost of sales [k]; if the range runs near the current 45% margin while revenue passes $840,000, it adds profitable sales rather than diluting margins [app].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin shows profitability after cost of sales, before expenses
Gross profit margin can be compared across periods or product lines to judge cost control
application_max_2: Applies 45% this year from $378,000 / $840,000
Applies last year's 39% from $304,200 / $780,000 and weighs margin against $840,000 revenue

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using gross profit margin alone to judge the own-brand proposal.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: gross profit margin ignores operating expenses [k]; with expenses of $252,000, the profit margin is only 15% ($126,000 divided by $840,000), so judging the range on the $378,000 gross profit alone could approve a proposal that actually cuts final profit [app][an]. Limitation 2: gross profit margin is calculated from historic figures and ignores other evidence [k]; last year's $304,200 and this year's $378,000 say nothing about how customers respond to cheaper own-brand clothing in one of the 3 stores, so sales and cash forecasts must also be studied [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin ignores expenses / overhead costs
Gross profit margin is historic and ignores non-financial evidence
application_max_2: Applies $252,000 expenses to show profit margin is only 15% ($126,000 / $840,000)
Applies historic figures such as $304,200 and $378,000 and the 3 stores context
analysis_max_2: Explains a proposal can raise gross profit yet cut final profit once expenses are charged
Explains historic margins cannot predict customer response to the cheaper range

questions.question_text: Do you think Naomi should launch the cheaper own-brand range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Naomi could launch the range because demand from price-sensitive customers is often strong in clothing retail [k]. Revenue growing from $780,000 to $840,000 with a 45% gross profit margin shows Marlbrook can price own-brand lines below the premium tier and still cover the cost of sales, potentially lifting volume and profit together [app][an]. However, expenses of $252,000 leave a profit margin of only 15% ($126,000 divided by $840,000), so heavy discounting on the own-brand range could cut overall profit even as sales rise [app][an]. Conversely, keeping premium lines protects the margin gain from 39% to 45% and the rise from $97,500 to $126,000, but cedes the value segment to rivals [k][eval]. Overall, Naomi should trial the own-brand range in one of the 3 stores for one quarter, comparing its margin against 45% before wider roll-out; expand only if final profit holds above this year's $126,000, because the thin 15% profit margin leaves little room for error [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Gross profit margin improved from 39% to 45%; profit margin is 15% ($126,000 / $840,000)
Revenue grew from $780,000 to $840,000; expenses remain high at $252,000
application_max_2: Applies the 45% margin headroom and 15% profit margin to the range pricing decision
Applies revenue growth from $780,000 to $840,000 as evidence of demand
analysis_max_2: Explains that value demand and margin headroom could lift volume and profit together
Explains that discounting could cut final profit even if sales rise because expenses are fixed at $252,000
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation weighing margin protection against new demand, tied to a one-store trial and the $126,000 profit benchmark

scenario_stem:
Halvern Castings Ltd is a private limited company founded 9 years ago by Marcus Bellamy, casting iron brackets for farm machinery in a Country X factory employing 46 workers. At 30 June it held current assets of $286,000, comprising inventories of $150,000, trade receivables of $96,000 and cash of $40,000, against current liabilities of $104,000 to suppliers and the bank.

The main steel supplier has offered a 2% cash discount if Halvern settles the $60,000 early rather than on the usual 60-day terms. Marcus is deciding whether to take a 90-day bank loan at 1.5% interest to pay early, or to wait for the normal settlement date and risk upsetting the supplier before steel prices in Country X rise again next quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'current ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities with its current assets, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities; Halvern Castings holds $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities, a ratio of 2.75:1. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
It shows the liquidity of the business, i.e. its ability to pay short-term debts

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Marcus should check the current ratio before taking the loan.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities [k]; Halvern's $286,000 of current assets against $104,000 of current liabilities is 2.75:1, indicating comfortable cover today before taking on a 90-day loan [app]. Reason 2: the current ratio helps Marcus see whether paying $60,000 early still leaves the business able to meet its remaining bills [k]; paying early would use the $40,000 cash plus part of the $96,000 trade receivables, so he must confirm cover stays above 1:1 through the 90 days [app].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio shows whether current assets cover current liabilities
Current ratio indicates the liquidity buffer available before taking on new short-term debt
application_max_2: Applies the $40,000 cash and $96,000 trade receivables against the $60,000 early payment

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the current ratio alone for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the current ratio treats all current assets as equally quick to convert into cash [k]; Halvern holds $150,000 of inventories, the slowest asset, so excluding them (the acid test ratio) gives a more cautious picture of ($286,000 minus $150,000) divided by $104,000, about 1.31:1 [app][an]. Limitation 2: the current ratio is a single snapshot at 30 June and ignores timing [k]; if $96,000 of trade receivables pay slowly, Halvern may not have the $60,000 in cash even though the 2.75:1 ratio looks strong, so cash-flow timing must also be checked [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio assumes all current assets convert to cash equally fast
Current ratio is a static snapshot and ignores cash-flow timing
application_max_2: Applies the $150,000 inventories exclusion giving an acid test of about 1.31:1
Applies the $96,000 trade receivables timing and the 2.75:1 snapshot
analysis_max_2: Explains inventories are the slowest asset so the current ratio overstates true liquidity
Explains that a strong snapshot figure can still hide a cash-timing shortfall in the 90 days

questions.question_text: Do you think Marcus should take the 90-day bank loan to pay the supplier early? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Marcus could take the loan because a strong steel supplier supports reliable deliveries for the farm-machinery brackets his factory casts [k]. The 2% discount on the $60,000 saves $1,200 against $900 of interest (1.5% for 90 days), a net gain of $300, and the current ratio of 2.75:1 plus an acid test of about 1.31:1 shows he can cover a short 90-day loan from $286,000 of current assets [app][an]. However, the cash buffer is only $40,000 and the $96,000 of trade receivables must convert to cash within 90 days, so if customers pay late the loan rolls over with fresh interest and the net gain turns into a loss [app][an]. Conversely, waiting for the normal 60-day settlement costs nothing but forfeits the $1,200 discount and leaves the supplier waiting [k][eval]. Overall, Marcus should take the loan only if receivables have a strong payment record and the supplier confirms the terms in writing; the acid test of about 1.31:1 supports it, but with only a $300 net saving he should walk away if any part of the arrangement looks uncertain [eval].

knowledge_max_2: 2% discount on $60,000 = $1,200 saved; 1.5% for 90 days = $900 interest; net $300
Current ratio 2.75:1; acid test about 1.31:1; cash buffer only $40,000
application_max_2: Applies the $1,200 saving versus $900 interest and net $300 gain
Applies the $40,000 cash and $96,000 receivables against the 90-day repayment window
analysis_max_2: Explains receivables converting on time is essential or the loan rolls over costing more
Explains the liquidity ratios support a short-term loan from current assets
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to written confirmation, receivables' payment record and the thin $300 net benefit

scenario_stem:
Tidewater Leisure Pools Ltd is a private limited company operating 2 swimming and fitness venues in Country X, directed by Rachel Achebe for 6 years. In the year to 31 August, profit was $180,000 and capital employed was $900,000; last year profit was $135,000 with capital employed of $900,000, and a nearby competitor achieves an ROCE of 12% across its larger chain of 4 venues.

Rachel must decide whether to build a third venue costing $400,000 from retained profit, expected to add only $52,000 in the first year but $112,000 once fully established, or to increase dividends of $60,000 a year payable to shareholders who have supported the company since it floated 6 years ago. The decision will be announced at the annual general meeting in September.

questions.question_text: Calculate the Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) for Tidewater Leisure Pools. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: ROCE is the percentage return a business earns on the capital invested in its operations, calculated as profit divided by capital employed multiplied by 100; Tidewater Leisure Pools earns $180,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100 = 20.0% this year, up from 15.0% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000 multiplied by 100). [2]

knowledge_max_2: ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100
It shows how effectively capital is used to generate profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why ROCE is the key figure for the board's decision.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: ROCE shows how much profit each dollar of capital employed generates [k]; Tidewater's ROCE improved from 15% last year ($135,000 divided by $900,000) to 20% this year ($180,000 divided by $900,000), well above the competitor's 12%, evidence that the existing venues earn strong returns [app]. Reason 2: ROCE lets the board compare the $400,000 third venue with leaving retained profit idle or paying dividends [k]; if the new venue lifts annual profit towards $292,000 in its third year, ROCE would reach about 22.5% ($292,000 divided by $1,300,000), beating the competitor and justifying the build [app].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE shows the return generated on capital employed
ROCE allows investment options to be compared on a percentage return basis
application_max_2: Applies 20.0% this year ($180,000 / $900,000) versus 15.0% last year and 12% competitor
Applies the $400,000 venue cost, $1,300,000 resulting capital employed and the $292,000 third-year profit potential

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ROCE is based on historic figures and profit only, not on how long the $400,000 takes to recover [k]; the venue adds only $52,000 in its first year, giving a first-year ROCE of about 17.8% on capital employed of $1,300,000, so early years dilute the ratio before the full benefit appears [app][an]. Limitation 2: ROCE ignores the other factors affecting the 2 existing venues [k]; occupancy, local competition and the $60,000 dividend expectation do not appear in the ratio, so customer demand and team capacity must also guide the board [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE is historic and does not show how an investment recovers its cost over time
ROCE ignores non-financial and contextual factors
application_max_2: Applies the $52,000 first-year contribution and the $1,300,000 resulting capital employed (about 17.8%)
Applies the $400,000 cost, $60,000 dividends and the 2 existing venues context
analysis_max_2: Explains that first-year returns dilute ROCE so the ratio looks worse than the long-run position
Explains that ROCE cannot capture demand, competition or shareholder expectations

questions.question_text: Do you think Rachel should build the third venue? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Rachel could approve the build because the business currently earns an ROCE of 20% ($180,000 divided by $900,000) against a competitor's 12%, proving the 2-venue model works well [k][app]. The third venue should add $52,000 in year one and $112,000 at maturity, lifting capital employed to $1,300,000 and reaching an ROCE of about 22.5% in year three, while also defending the venues' position in Country X [an]. However, first-year ROCE falls to about 17.8% ($232,000 divided by $1,300,000), and paying $400,000 from retained profit reduces dividends below the $60,000 shareholders currently expect [app][an]. Conversely, paying larger dividends rewards shareholders now but leaves $400,000 barely generating anything and loses the chance to outgrow the 12% competitor [k][eval]. Overall, Rachel should approve the third venue but phase the spending, because a long-run ROCE above the competitor matters more than short-term dilution, provided membership numbers stay strong and some dividend is maintained during construction [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Current ROCE 20% ($180,000 / $900,000); competitor 12%; last year 15%
Third venue: $52,000 year one, $112,000 at maturity; capital employed rises to $1,300,000
application_max_2: Applies the 20% current ROCE versus the competitor's 12% as evidence the model works
Applies the first-year 17.8% ROCE ($232,000 / $1,300,000) and the dividend cut below $60,000
analysis_max_2: Explains that maturity-phase profit lifts ROCE to about 22.5% and defends market position
Explains that short-term dilution and dividend cuts are the main shareholder costs
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to long-run ROCE superiority, dividend affordability and membership strength

scenario_stem:
Redfern Farm Kitchen Ltd is a private limited company founded 5 years ago, producing jars of pasta sauce and pesto from a Country X factory with 18 staff. In the year to 30 April, revenue was $610,000, gross profit $183,000, expenses $103,700 and profit $79,300; last year revenue was $520,000, gross profit $171,600, expenses $88,400 and profit $83,200.

Revenue has grown by $90,000, yet profits have fallen. The value range launched 18 months ago now accounts for 60% of jars sold. The founder, Colin Marsh, is deciding whether to discontinue the value range and focus on premium sauces, or keep it for the volume it brings and the shelf space it wins in supermarkets in 3 supermarket chains across Country X.

questions.question_text: Calculate the profit margin for Redfern Farm Kitchen. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: Profit margin (net profit margin) is the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all expenses are deducted, calculated as profit divided by revenue multiplied by 100; Redfern Farm Kitchen earned $79,300 divided by $610,000 multiplied by 100 = 13.0% this year, down from 16.0% last year ($83,200 divided by $520,000 multiplied by 100). [2]

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin = profit / revenue x 100
It shows the percentage of each dollar of revenue left as final profit after expenses

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Colin should study the profit margin before discontinuing the value range.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the profit margin shows the percentage of revenue left after all expenses, revealing whether the value range is truly profitable [k]; the margin fell from 16.0% last year ($83,200 divided by $520,000) to 13.0% this year ($79,300 divided by $610,000), a drop of 3 percentage points despite revenue growing by $90,000 [app]. Reason 2: the profit margin shows whether the value range dilutes overall profitability [k]; with the value range making 60% of jars sold and expenses rising from $88,400 to $103,700, overhead growth is eating into final profit even though gross profit held near 30% [app].

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin shows final profitability after expenses
Profit margin can be compared across periods to detect dilution of profit
application_max_2: Applies the 60% value-range share of jars and expenses rising from $88,400 to $103,700

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using profit margin to judge the value range.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the profit margin is a single blended figure that cannot split value-range performance from premium-sauce performance [k]; without product-level accounts, the 13.0% margin could hide a strong premium line subsidising a weak value line, so discontinuing the wrong lines would remove volume without lifting profit [app][an]. Limitation 2: the profit margin ignores the strategic value the range brings [k]; 60% of jars sold means the value lines fill factory capacity and support the $90,000 of revenue growth, and dropping them could strand overheads while gross profit margin stays at 30% [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin is a blended figure and cannot isolate product-line performance
Profit margin ignores strategic and volume effects
application_max_2: Applies the 13.0% blended margin and missing product-level breakdown
Applies the 60% of jars sold, the 30% gross profit margin and $90,000 revenue growth
analysis_max_2: Explains that without line-level data the wrong decision could be made
Explains that dropping the range could strand overheads and lose revenue growth

questions.question_text: Do you think Colin should discontinue the value range? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Colin could keep the range because it accounts for 60% of jars sold and helped revenue grow by $90,000 (from $520,000 to $610,000), filling factory capacity and widening brand reach in Country X [k][app]. Dropping it might restore the profit margin above 16% but risks losing most of the volume that absorbs factory overheads [an]. However, the profit margin has fallen to 13.0% ($79,300) and expenses are $103,700 (up from $88,400), so the value range may be turning a healthy 30% gross profit margin into thin final profit while tying up cash in stock and distribution [app][an]. Conversely, focusing on premium sauces could restore profit above $83,200, but below that the value lines still absorb fixed overhead that premium sales alone may not carry [k][eval]. Overall, Colin should re-price the value range and cut its costs first rather than discontinue it outright, because 60% of volume is too important to drop without product-level profit evidence, but he should review discontinuation if margins do not recover within 12 months [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Profit margin fell from 16.0% to 13.0% ($83,200 to $79,300); expenses rose $88,400 to $103,700
Revenue grew by $90,000; value range is 60% of jars sold; gross profit margin 30%
application_max_2: Applies the 60% volume share and $90,000 revenue growth to argue for keeping the range
Applies the 13.0% margin and $103,700 expenses to argue for discontinuation
analysis_max_2: Explains that dropping the range risks losing volume and overhead absorption
Explains that the range converts 30% gross profit into thin final profit
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation of re-pricing and cost-cutting first with a 12-month review before discontinuation

scenario_stem:
Thorne & Vale Toys Ltd is a private limited company operating a toy shop in Country X, established 7 years ago by sisters Beth and Maya Cole. At 31 October, current assets were $340,000 (inventories $224,000, trade receivables $88,000 and cash $28,000) against current liabilities of $160,000 owed to suppliers and the landlord. Last year the acid test ratio was 0.95:1, and festive season sales usually make up 45% of annual toy sales.

With the festive season approaching, Beth is deciding whether to place the full festive supplier order of $180,000 of stock now, backed by her sales forecast, or a reduced order of $120,000, waiting to see how the first half of December trading goes before reordering. The supplier's prices rise by 6% in November, which Beth wants to factor in.

questions.question_text: Define 'acid test ratio'.
questions.model_answer: The acid test ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities using only its quick assets (excluding inventories), calculated as (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities; Thorne & Vale Toys has ($340,000 minus $224,000) divided by $160,000 = $116,000 divided by $160,000 = 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1 last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio = (current assets - inventories) / current liabilities
It measures immediate liquidity without relying on selling inventories

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Beth should consider the acid test ratio before placing the festive order.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the acid test ratio shows whether liquid assets alone can cover current liabilities, without counting inventories [k]; Thorne's quick assets are only $116,000 ($88,000 receivables plus $28,000 cash) against $160,000 of current liabilities, giving 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1 last year [app]. Reason 2: the acid test ratio signals whether the full $180,000 stock order would stretch the business through the festive peak [k]; festive sales make up 45% of annual toy sales, so stock must be right, but committing $180,000 against a $44,000 shortfall exposes the shop to supplier-payment risk [app].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio shows liquidity excluding inventories
Acid test ratio indicates the risk of committing to large stock purchases on credit
application_max_2: Applies the $116,000 quick assets against $160,000 liabilities = 0.725:1, down from 0.95:1
Applies the $180,000 order against only $28,000 cash and the $44,000 shortfall

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using the acid test ratio for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the acid test ratio assumes inventories cannot be sold quickly, which is rarely true in a busy toy shop in December [k]; festive stock turns over fast, so excluding all $224,000 of inventories may understate Thorne's ability to generate cash from the 45% of annual toy sales that arrive in the season [app][an]. Limitation 2: the acid test ratio is a single snapshot and ignores the effect of order size on December sales [k]; a reduced order of $120,000 protects cash but could leave shelves empty in the peak fortnight when 45% of annual toy sales are made, losing revenue and emptying shelves [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio assumes inventories cannot be converted to cash quickly
Acid test ratio is a snapshot and ignores sales momentum and timing
application_max_2: Applies the $224,000 inventories exclusion and the 45% festive sales share
Applies the $120,000 reduced order versus the $180,000 full order scenario
analysis_max_2: Explains that fast-turning festive stock means the ratio understates real cash generation
Explains that a reduced order risks lost festive sales despite protecting cash

questions.question_text: Do you think Beth should place the full $180,000 festive order? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Beth could place the full order because festive season sales make up 45% of annual toy sales, and running out of stock in December would forfeit her biggest trading period of the year [k][app]. The overall current ratio of 2.125:1 ($340,000 divided by $160,000) shows comfortable cover, and festive stock should convert quickly to cash if December trading matches the 45% pattern [an]. However, the acid test ratio of 0.725:1 means quick assets of $116,000 fall $44,000 short of current liabilities, and a full $180,000 order on top of a cash balance of $28,000 means paying suppliers before festive revenue arrives, risking overdraft costs [app][an]. Conversely, a reduced order of $120,000 saves $60,000 of cash and protects the shop if festive sales disappoint, though re-ordering mid-season may delay delivery and cost late-December sales [k][eval]. Overall, Beth should place a staged order: most of the $180,000 now with a top-up in early December once first-week festive cash arrives; this balances the 0.725:1 acid test against the 45% of annual toy sales at stake [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Festive season sales make up 45% of annual toy sales; acid test 0.725:1 versus 0.95:1 last year
Current ratio 2.125:1; quick assets $116,000 vs liabilities $160,000 ($44,000 shortfall); cash only $28,000
application_max_2: Applies the 45% festive sales share and 2.125:1 current ratio to argue for ordering
Applies the 0.725:1 acid test, $44,000 shortfall and $28,000 cash to argue caution
analysis_max_2: Explains festive stock converts quickly to cash if December trading is normal
Explains supplier payments fall due before festive revenue arrives, risking overdraft
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation of a staged order balancing acid test risk against the 45% festive revenue at stake

scenario_stem:
Fenland Woollens Ltd is a private limited company manufacturing woollen blankets in Country X, with a city mill and a smaller rural branch opened 5 years ago. In the year to 30 June, the city mill earned revenue of $540,000, gross profit of $167,400 and profit of $59,400 on capital employed of $594,000; the rural branch earned revenue of $300,000, gross profit of $66,000 and profit of $9,000 on capital employed of $225,000.

The board wants to close the rural branch if the figures confirm it is dragging performance. However, the branch supplies specialist yarn to the city mill, employs 15 local weavers, and its closure would affect the whole community. The managing director must present her recommendation at next month's board meeting.

questions.question_text: State two limitations of ratio analysis.
questions.model_answer: Two limitations of ratio analysis are firstly that ratios are based on historic figures and may not reflect future performance, and secondly that ratios ignore qualitative factors such as staff morale, customer loyalty and community impact, so they cannot tell the whole story about a business. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Ratios use historic data, so they may not predict future performance
Ratios ignore qualitative and non-financial factors

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the board has used ratio analysis on the two mills' figures.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: ratio analysis lets the board compare the two mills on a common basis [k]; the city mill produced a 31% gross profit margin ($167,400 divided by $540,000) against the rural branch's 22% ($66,000 divided by $300,000), showing the rural branch is weaker at the making or buying stage [app]. Use 2: ratio analysis highlights where profit leaks after expenses [k]; the rural branch returned only a 3% profit margin ($9,000 divided by $300,000) on capital employed of $225,000 (an ROCE of 4%) versus 11% and 10% for the city mill, flagging underperformance for the board [app].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis enables comparison of different parts of a business on a common basis
Ratio analysis identifies weaknesses in profitability and efficiency
application_max_2: Applies 31% vs 22% gross profit margins ($167,400/$540,000 vs $66,000/$300,000)
Applies 3% vs 11% profit margins and 4% vs 10% ROCE ($9,000/$225,000 vs $59,400/$594,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of ratio analysis that apply to this closure decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ratios ignore the qualitative factors behind the figures [k]; the rural branch supplies specialist yarn to the city mill, so closing it could disrupt the city mill's 31% gross profit margin in ways that appear nowhere in the rural branch's own 3% profit margin [app][an]. Limitation 2: ratios are calculated from one year's figures and give no reasons for the poor result [k]; one weak year of $9,000 profit does not prove the branch cannot improve with new equipment or markets, and the value of 15 local weavers' skills to the Country X community is invisible to the ratios [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratios ignore qualitative and interconnected business factors
Ratios are historic single-year snapshots with no explanation of causes
application_max_2: Applies the rural branch's yarn supply role versus the city mill's 31% gross profit margin
Applies the 15 local weavers, $9,000 profit and single-year data
analysis_max_2: Explains closure could damage the profitable city mill despite good city ratios
Explains that ratios cannot explain or reverse the underlying causes of weak performance

questions.question_text: Do you think the managing director should recommend closing the rural branch? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The director could recommend closure because the figures are stark: the rural branch returned a 3% profit margin ($9,000 divided by $300,000) and a 4% ROCE ($9,000 divided by $225,000), far below the city mill's 11% profit margin and 10% ROCE [k][app]. Closing would release the $225,000 of capital employed to be used in the city mill, which earns $167,400 of gross profit on $540,000 revenue [an]. However, the branch supplies specialist yarn to the city mill; closure could raise city mill's costs and endanger its 31% gross profit margin, and making 15 local weavers redundant damages the yarn supply and community goodwill [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the branch open preserves the yarn supply and the weavers' skills, but it consumed management time for only $9,000 profit, while the same $225,000 employed in the city mill would earn about 10% [k][eval]. Overall, the director should not close the branch outright; she should set a 12-month turnaround plan targeting yarn costs and sales, because the supply dependency outweighs one year of weak ratios, but closure must follow if branch profit stays below, say, $30,000 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Rural branch: 3% profit margin, 4% ROCE ($9,000 / $225,000); city mill: 11% and 10%
City mill gross profit $167,400 on $540,000 revenue (31%)
application_max_2: Applies the stark 3%/4% rural versus 11%/10% city ratios to argue for closure
Applies the yarn supply role and 15 local weavers to argue against closure
analysis_max_2: Explains released capital employed could earn the city mill's higher return
Explains closure could disrupt the city mill and endanger its 31% gross profit margin
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation of a 12-month turnaround with a profit trigger for closure

scenario_stem:
Marrow Lane Catering Ltd is a private limited company providing event catering across Country X, directed by Tom Alvarez for 10 years with 26 staff and a loyal base of corporate clients. At 30 September, current assets were $408,000 (cash $240,000, trade receivables $108,000 and inventories $60,000) against current liabilities of $120,000; last year the current ratio was 2.1:1.

A bank holds a $300,000 loan against the business at 7% interest. Shareholders want Tom to repay $240,000 of the loan early from cash reserves to save interest, or to keep the cash as a buffer for a large spring wedding contract that needs $90,000 of catering supplies paid up front by February. The bank has hinted it might extend the loan if needed.

questions.question_text: Calculate the current ratio for Marrow Lane Catering. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: The current ratio measures current assets against current liabilities, calculated as current assets divided by current liabilities; Marrow Lane Catering holds $408,000 divided by $120,000 = 3.4:1, up from 2.1:1 last year. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities
Expressing the answer as a ratio such as 3.4:1

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of a strong current ratio for the wedding contract.
questions.model_answer: Benefit 1: a strong current ratio shows Marrow Lane can pay its short-term obligations as they fall due [k]; with $408,000 of current assets against $120,000 of current liabilities (3.4:1), the business can comfortably cover the $90,000 of up-front wedding supplies and normal monthly bills [app]. Benefit 2: a healthy current ratio reassures suppliers and the lender of creditworthiness [k]; paying the $90,000 of catering supplies up front is easy when cash alone is $240,000, and the ratio gives the bank confidence about the $300,000 loan [app].

knowledge_max_2: A strong current ratio indicates the business can meet short-term obligations
A healthy current ratio strengthens credibility with suppliers and lenders
application_max_2: Applies $408,000 / $120,000 = 3.4:1 against the $90,000 up-front wedding supplies
Applies the $240,000 cash and the $300,000 bank loan context

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of a very high current ratio.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: a very high current ratio can mean resources are idle rather than productive [k]; $240,000 of cash earning nothing while the $300,000 loan still costs 7% interest ($21,000 a year) represents an opportunity cost shareholders rightly question [app][an]. Limitation 2: the current ratio hides what the assets actually are [k]; if most of the $408,000 were slow-moving inventories or unpaid trade receivables of $108,000 rather than cash, the 3.4:1 ratio would overstate true short-term strength [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: A high current ratio may indicate idle, unproductive resources
The current ratio does not show the composition or quality of current assets
application_max_2: Applies the $240,000 idle cash against the 7% interest on the $300,000 loan ($21,000 a year)
Applies the $60,000 inventories and $108,000 trade receivables composition of the $408,000
analysis_max_2: Explains idle cash loses value against the ongoing loan interest cost
Explains the ratio can flatter liquidity if assets are slow-moving

questions.question_text: Do you think Tom should repay $240,000 of the loan early? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Tom could repay the $240,000 because it would save $16,800 of annual interest at 7%, directly lifting profit, and shareholders would see disciplined use of cash instead of a 3.4:1 idle balance [k][app]. The reduced current ratio of 1.4:1 ($168,000 divided by $120,000) still covers current liabilities, and the loan balance would fall to $60,000, lightening the balance sheet and reducing risk [an]. However, using all $240,000 of cash leaves nothing as a buffer if the spring wedding contract needs $90,000 of supplies up front or if receivables of $108,000 pay late, and Tom could face emergency borrowing at higher cost [app][an]. Conversely, keeping the cash protects the wedding contract and day-to-day operations, but shareholders would question why a 7% loan stays outstanding while cash sits idle [k][eval]. Overall, Tom should repay $180,000 now and keep $60,000 plus receivables as a buffer; this saves about $12,600 of interest, keeps the current ratio near 1.9:1 ($228,000 divided by $120,000), and still funds the wedding supplies, balancing shareholder pressure against operational safety [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Repaying $240,000 at 7% saves $16,800 a year; repaying $180,000 saves about $12,600
Post-repayment current ratio: 1.4:1 (full repayment) or about 1.9:1 ($228,000/$120,000) for $180,000
application_max_2: Applies the $16,800 interest saving and reduced 1.4:1 ratio to argue for repayment
Applies the $90,000 wedding supplies need and $108,000 receivables to argue for keeping cash
analysis_max_2: Explains repayment lifts profit and lightens the balance sheet
Explains zero cash risks emergency borrowing if the wedding contract is delayed or receivables pay late
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation of a partial $180,000 repayment keeping a buffer and a near-1.9:1 ratio

scenario_stem:
Pellham Bay Hotel Ltd is a private limited company running a 120-room coastal hotel in Country X, employing 85 staff. It borrowed to fund a new wing of 30 rooms, a $1.8 million investment, so capital employed rose from $2.0 million to $3.8 million in the year to 31 July. Profit rose from $400,000 to $570,000, yet room occupancy averaged only 62%, and the hotel industry average ROCE is 14%.

The managing director must decide whether to approve a Phase 2 extension costing $1.5 million, adding 24 more rooms, or pause expansion and let the first wing fill up before committing more capital to the project or upgrading the original 90 hotel rooms. Shareholders will watch this decision closely this year.

questions.question_text: Define 'return on capital employed' (ROCE).
questions.model_answer: Return on capital employed measures the percentage return a business earns on the capital invested in its operations, calculated as profit divided by capital employed multiplied by 100; Pellham Bay Hotel earned $570,000 divided by $3.8 million multiplied by 100 = 15.0% this year, down from 20.0% last year ($400,000 divided by $2.0 million). [2]

knowledge_max_2: ROCE = profit / capital employed x 100
It shows how efficiently capital invested in the business is turned into profit

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the managing director should worry about the falling ROCE before Phase 2.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: ROCE shows the return the hotel earns on each dollar of capital employed [k]; it fell from 20% last year ($400,000 divided by $2.0 million) to 15% ($570,000 divided by $3.8 million), even though profit rose, showing the borrowed $1.8 million wing is not yet earning its keep [app]. Reason 2: ROCE lets the director benchmark the hotel against the industry average of 14% [k]; at 15% Pellham barely beats that benchmark, so adding a further $1.5 million in Phase 2 without higher occupancy risks ROCE slipping below the industry average [app].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE measures the percentage return on capital employed
ROCE can be benchmarked against competitors or industry averages
application_max_2: Applies the 14% industry average and the $1.5 million Phase 2 cost

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of using ROCE to judge the new wing's performance.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ROCE uses balance-sheet figures and historic carrying values, not what the wing could be worth now [k]; if property values have risen above the $3.8 million carrying value, the 15% ROCE understates the wing's true return [app][an]. Limitation 2: ROCE ignores non-financial measures that explain performance [k]; occupancy of only 62% and the cost of servicing the borrowed money do not appear in the ratio, so Phase 2 must also weigh occupancy trends and borrowing risk [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: ROCE uses carrying values that may differ from market values
ROCE ignores non-financial measures and financing details
application_max_2: Applies the $3.8 million carrying value versus possible market appreciation of the wing
Applies the 62% occupancy and the borrowed-money funding of the $1.8 million wing
analysis_max_2: Explains historic carrying values can understate the true return on the wing
Explains occupancy and borrowing costs drive the investment decision beyond the ratio

questions.question_text: Do you think the managing director should approve the Phase 2 extension? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The director could approve Phase 2 because the first wing lifted profit from $400,000 to $570,000 (up $170,000, or 42.5%) and the ROCE of 15% still edges the industry average of 14%, showing the strategy works once the rooms fill [k][app]. Adding 24 rooms for $1.5 million would spread fixed costs over more guests and could lift profit and ROCE if occupancy climbs above 62% [an]. However, occupancy of only 62% means the new 30-room wing is already under-filled; adding a further 24 rooms could push ROCE below 14% and deepen the exposure to borrowed money beyond the $1.8 million already owed [app][an]. Conversely, pausing Phase 2 delays expansion but protects the existing 15% ROCE and cash flow, letting the first wing fill until profit and ROCE recover toward 20% [k][eval]. Overall, the director should not approve Phase 2 yet; she should wait until occupancy exceeds about 75% and the wing proves it can hold an ROCE comfortably above the 14% industry average, because committing a further $1.5 million at 62% occupancy risks diluting shareholder returns further [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Profit rose $400,000 to $570,000 (up 42.5%); ROCE fell 20% to 15% but still beats the 14% industry average
Phase 2 costs $1.5 million for 24 rooms; occupancy is only 62%
application_max_2: Applies the $570,000 profit and 15% ROCE versus the 14% industry average to argue for approval
Applies 62% occupancy and the extra $1.5 million borrowed to argue against
analysis_max_2: Explains spreading fixed costs over more rooms could lift profit and ROCE
Explains adding rooms at 62% occupancy risks pushing ROCE below the industry average
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to defer Phase 2 until occupancy exceeds about 75% and ROCE holds above 14%

scenario_stem:
Farlow Wholesale Foods Ltd is a private limited company supplying chilled and frozen foods to corner shops in Country X, run by director Samira Iqbal for 4 years with a depot and fleet of 9 delivery vans. At 30 June, current assets were $1,250,000 (inventories $980,000, trade receivables $180,000, cash $90,000) and current liabilities were $260,000; a competitor reports an acid test ratio of 1.6:1.

A national supermarket chain has offered a contract worth $400,000 a year, at a gross profit margin of 17%, if Farlow grants 60-day credit terms instead of its usual 30 days. Samira estimates debtors would rise by about $130,000. She must decide whether to accept the offer before the contract starts in September, because her usual 30-day terms have always kept payments simple.

questions.question_text: Calculate the acid test ratio for Farlow Wholesale Foods. Show your working.
questions.model_answer: The acid test ratio measures whether a business can meet its current liabilities using only its quick assets, calculated as (current assets minus inventories) divided by current liabilities; Farlow Wholesale Foods has ($1,250,000 minus $980,000) divided by $260,000 = $270,000 divided by $260,000, about 1.04:1, below the competitor's 1.6:1. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio = (current assets - inventories) / current liabilities
Expressing the answer as a ratio such as about 1.04:1

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the acid test ratio matters for the 60-day credit offer.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: the acid test ratio shows whether Farlow can meet current liabilities without selling inventories [k]; excluding the $980,000 of inventories, quick assets are $270,000 ($180,000 receivables plus $90,000 cash) against $260,000 of current liabilities, giving about 1.04:1, well below the competitor's 1.6:1 [app]. Reason 2: the acid test ratio reveals how tight cash is before granting longer credit [k]; granting 60-day terms on the $400,000 contract would add about $130,000 of debtors at any time, lifting the paper ratio but stranding the cash Farlow needs to pay its own suppliers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio shows liquidity without relying on inventory sales
Acid test ratio highlights how much cash is tied up in receivables
application_max_2: Applies the $270,000 quick assets / $260,000 liabilities = about 1.04:1 versus competitor's 1.6:1
Applies the $130,000 extra debtors on 60-day terms and the $90,000 cash

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of the acid test ratio for this decision.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: the acid test ratio treats all receivables as equally collectable [k]; the national supermarket chain is almost certainly a reliable payer, so discounting its $130,000 from quick assets may understate Farlow's true liquidity under the new 60-day terms [app][an]. Limitation 2: the acid test ratio is a snapshot and ignores the timing and profit impact of the contract [k]; the $400,000 contract earns about $68,000 of annual gross profit at 17% and cash would arrive within 60 to 90 days, so the ratio alone cannot capture whether the deal strengthens the business [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Acid test ratio treats all receivables as equal, ignoring creditworthiness
Acid test ratio is a snapshot ignoring timing and profit effects
application_max_2: Applies the $130,000 new supermarket debtors against the reliable-payer assumption
Applies the $400,000 contract at 17% gross profit margin (about $68,000) and 60 to 90 day collection
analysis_max_2: Explains reliable supermarket debts make the ratio understate true liquidity
Explains the snapshot cannot weigh the profit and timing benefits of the contract

questions.question_text: Do you think Samira should accept the supermarket contract on 60-day terms? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Samira could accept because the $400,000 annual contract earns about $68,000 of gross profit at 17%, and 60-day terms are standard for supermarket supply deals, strengthening Farlow's credibility with a national chain [k][app]. Even with debtors rising by about $130,000, the acid test ratio would move from 1.04:1 to about 1.54:1, close to the competitor's 1.6:1, and the supermarket's payment record makes collection risk low [an]. However, cash of only $90,000 against $260,000 of current liabilities means Farlow relies on quick collection; if the supermarket pays late or queries invoices, suppliers pressing for cash could strain the business despite the profitable contract [app][an]. Conversely, declining keeps the 30-day terms and simple liquidity, but it forfeits $400,000 of revenue and the $68,000 gross profit, which would likely go to a rival supplier [k][eval]. Overall, Samira should accept the contract but negotiate a shorter first cycle (for example 45 days for the opening quarter) or a deposit as a condition, because the $68,000 gross profit outweighs the timing cost if collection risk is controlled up front [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Contract $400,000 at 17% gross profit margin = about $68,000 gross profit; 60-day vs 30-day terms
Acid test would rise from 1.04:1 to about 1.54:1 with $130,000 extra debtors; competitor 1.6:1
application_max_2: Applies the $68,000 gross profit and 1.54:1 projected acid test to argue for acceptance
Applies the $90,000 cash and $260,000 current liabilities to argue for caution
analysis_max_2: Explains supermarket reliability makes collection risk low and the ratio stays near competitor level
Explains late payment or invoice queries could strain suppliers despite profitability
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation to accept with negotiated 45-day opening cycle or deposit to control collection risk

scenario_stem:
Fallowfield & Dean Licensed Grocers Ltd is a private limited company running 2 convenience stores in Country X, owned by cousins Priya and Danny Fallowfield. In the year to 30 April, revenue was $800,000, gross profit $304,000, expenses $232,000 and profit $72,000; capital employed was $960,000 and current assets of $288,000 included inventories of $128,000, against current liabilities of $160,000.

The cousins want a $350,000 bank loan at 9% interest to refit both stores, improve refrigeration and add a chilled food counter. Alternatively, they could refit slowly over 3 years from retained profit. The bank has asked for ratio analysis from their accountant before deciding whether to approve the loan for the full amount requested. The cousins must satisfy the bank's lending committee in December.

questions.question_text: Identify two uses of ratio analysis.
questions.model_answer: Two uses of ratio analysis are firstly to compare a business's performance over time and against competitors, and secondly to support applications for finance such as bank loans by showing lenders the business's profitability and liquidity. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis compares performance over time or against competitors
Ratio analysis supports decisions and finance applications by quantifying profitability and liquidity

questions.question_text: Explain two ways ratio analysis can support the bank loan application.
questions.model_answer: Use 1: ratio analysis gives the bank a standardised view of creditworthiness [k]; the current ratio of 1.8:1 ($288,000 divided by $160,000) and an acid test ratio of 1.0:1 show the stores can cover short-term debts, supporting the $350,000 loan request [app]. Use 2: ratio analysis shows the owners understand their business numbers [k]; a gross profit margin of 38.0% ($304,000 divided by $800,000) and a 7.5% ROCE ($72,000 divided by $960,000) give the bank evidence the stores are profitable and professionally run [app].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis provides standardised evidence of creditworthiness
Ratio analysis demonstrates the owners understand their business performance
application_max_2: Applies the 1.8:1 current ratio and 1.0:1 acid test ratio ($288,000, $128,000, $160,000)
Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 7.5% ROCE ($304,000 / $800,000; $72,000 / $960,000)

questions.question_text: Explain two limitations of ratio analysis the cousins should consider.
questions.model_answer: Limitation 1: ratio analysis is based on historic accounts and cannot prove the refit will pay back [k]; a 9.0% profit margin ($72,000 divided by $800,000) would fall to about 5.1% after paying $31,500 of interest on the $350,000 loan (leaving $40,500 of profit), squeezing margins exactly when the stores need cash for the chilled counter [app][an]. Limitation 2: ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors and context [k]; neither the 38.0% gross profit margin nor the 1.8:1 current ratio captures customer loyalty, staffing stability or whether a chilled counter would actually lift sales, so the business plan matters as much as the figures [app][an].

knowledge_max_2: Ratio analysis is historic and cannot prove future returns on investment
Ratio analysis ignores qualitative factors such as customers and staff
application_max_2: Applies the 9.0% margin falling to about 5.1% after $31,500 interest ($40,500 profit)
Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin and 1.8:1 current ratio ignoring loyalty and the chilled counter
analysis_max_2: Explains interest costs sharply reduce final profit margin after borrowing
Explains figures alone cannot capture customer demand for the chilled counter

questions.question_text: Do you think the cousins should take the bank loan? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: The cousins could take the loan because refitting both stores now, rather than over 3 years from retained profit, defends the 38.0% gross profit margin ($304,000) against rivals adding chilled counters and captures sales sooner [k][app]. Profit of $72,000 (9.0% margin) barely covers the $31,500 interest, leaving $40,500 (5.1%), so the refit must generate meaningful new sales to be worthwhile [an]. However, the acid test ratio of 1.0:1 leaves no slack for trading setbacks, and capital employed would rise to $1,310,000, cutting ROCE to about 3.1% ($40,500 divided by $1,310,000) unless profits recover quickly [app][an]. Conversely, refitting slowly from retained profit avoids interest entirely and keeps the 1.0:1 acid test intact, but it cedes competitive advantage for 3 years and may never deliver the chilled food counter at all [k][eval]. Overall, the cousins should take the loan only if the bank offers a grace period before full repayments begin, because a 5.1% post-interest margin leaves almost no room for error; otherwise they should refit from retained profit and accept the slower refit as the safer route [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Loan $350,000 at 9% = $31,500 interest; post-interest profit $40,500 (5.1% margin)
ROCE falls to about 3.1% on $1,310,000 capital employed; acid test 1.0:1
application_max_2: Applies the $31,500 interest and 5.1% post-interest margin to argue for caution
Applies the 38.0% gross profit margin defence and acid test 1.0:1 to argue for slow refit
analysis_max_2: Explains the refit must lift sales enough to cover the $31,500 annual interest
Explains capital employed rises to $1,310,000 diluting ROCE to about 3.1%
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation tied to a bank grace period, otherwise slower retained-profit refit
